hook.line: Spanish is written the way it's said, almost perfectly. Learn about a dozen surprises and you can read any word aloud, starting with the first one you'll hear in Bogotá.
hook.en: Hi, how are you? (say it "OH-lah, KOH-moh ehs-TAHS")

examples.en: My name's Guillermo. (ll like the y in "yes"; gui is "ghee")
I'm from Medellín. ("meh-deh-YEEN": the mark says stress it here)
Nice to meet you, Jorge. (j is a breathy h: "HOR-heh")
Slower, please. ("des-PAH-syoh": c before i is an s)
I'm Tomás Herrera. (the rr is rolled, the last r is one quick tap)

rule:
Five vowels, one sound each, every time: *a* as in "father", *e* as in "bed", *i* as in "machine", *o* as in "or", *u* as in "rule".

The surprises: *h* is silent. *j*, and *g* before *e* or *i*, are a breathy h. *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes". *ñ* is the ny in "canyon". *b* and *v* sound the same. *z*, and *c* before *e* or *i*, are a plain s in Latin America. One *r* is a quick tap; *rr*, or an *r* that starts a word, is rolled. In *que*, *qui*, *gue* and *gui* the *u* is silent.

Stress: a word ending in a vowel, *n* or *s* stresses the second-to-last syllable (*co-lom-BIA-no*). Any other ending stresses the last one (*us-TED*). A written mark overrides both: *Bogotá*, *Tomás*. The mark is part of the spelling, and the app will check it.
smallPrint: The written mark is called a tilde (*la tilde*). It also tells apart pairs like *tú* (you) and *tu* (your), *sí* (yes) and *si* (if).
soundTip: Spanish vowels never glide. English "no" ends in a little "w"; Spanish *no* is clipped short: "noh", not "noh-oo". Same with the e in *me*: "meh", never "may".

options: *Vale* starts with the same sound as *bien*
The *rr* is rolled; the last *r* is one quick tap
*co-LOM-bya*: it ends in a vowel, so the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable
*rah-MOHN*: the mark moves the stress to the end

yourTurn.prompt: Type this with its accent mark, where the stress falls: *Soy de Bogota.*
yourTurn.why: *Bogotá* ends in a vowel but is stressed on the last syllable, so the *á* needs its mark.

yourTurn.prompt: Type this with its accent mark: *Soy de Medellin.* (It sounds like "meh-deh-YEEN".)
yourTurn.why: *Medellín* ends in *n*, so it would normally stress DE. The mark on *í* moves the stress to the end.

yourTurn.prompt: Type this with its accent mark: *Me llamo Tomas.*
yourTurn.why: *Tomás* ends in *s*, which would stress TO. The mark moves the stress to the last syllable.

yourTurn.prompt: Which letter spells the sound in "canyon"? Type the whole sentence: *Me llamo Toño* or *Me llamo Tono*?
yourTurn.why: The *ñ* is the ny in "canyon". Plain *n* would make it *TOH-noh*.

yourTurn.prompt: Which spelling is the one with the silent letter? Type the greeting that says "OH-lah": *Ola* or *Hola*?
yourTurn.why: The *h* is silent, so *Hola* is said "OH-lah". It is the spelling to type.

yourTurn.prompt: Type the sentence that a respelling describes: "soy deh meh-deh-YEEN".
yourTurn.why: The stress is on the last syllable, so the word needs its *í* mark.

yourTurn.prompt: Type the word that a respelling describes: "HOR-heh" (a name).
yourTurn.why: The breathy h sound is spelled *j* here, and *ge* is also breathy, so it is *Jorge*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type the sentence: "Slower, please", with the accent mark that stress needs on the first word.
yourTurn.why: *Más* carries a mark. *Despacio* needs none: it ends in a vowel and stresses PA.

pitfalls.why: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says BO-go-ta. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.
*ll* and *y* sound the same in most of Latin America, but the spelling still matters.
A question opens with *¿*, and *cómo* takes a mark when it's asking.

personal: Type your own name and your city the Spanish way: *Me llamo… Soy de…* Add any accent marks they need. Where would a Bogotano put the stress?
